# Bases for Dec

## When a fraction ends

A reduced fraction p/q ends (terminates) in base b only if every prime factor of q
divides b. Otherwise it repeats forever, whatever the precision.

| base | primes | ends | repeats |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2, 16 | 2 | halves, quarters | thirds, fifths |
| 6 | 2·3 | halves, thirds | fifths |
| 9 | 3² | thirds, ninths | halves, fifths |
| 10 | 2·5 | halves, fifths, tenths | thirds |
| 12 | 2²·3 | halves, thirds, quarters | fifths, tenths |
| 24 | 2³·3 | same set as 12 | fifths, tenths |
| 30, 60 | 2·3·5 | all of the above | sevenths |
| 10 + 9 tail | 2·5 · 3² | all of the above | sevenths |

- A numeral with n b10 digits and k b9 digits ends exactly when the reduced denominator
  divides 10ⁿ·9ᵏ. One b9 digit clears up to 3², two clear up to 3⁴.
- b10 + b9 ends every fraction whose denominator is 2ᵃ·3ᶜ·5ᵉ: the Babylonian "regular
  numbers", the same set as b60. b12 ends a strict subset of it (no fifths).
- No mix of 9, 10, 12, and 24 ends 1/7, 1/11, or 1/13.

## How many digits it takes

For a denominator 2ᵃ·3ᶜ:

| base | digits needed |
|---|---|
| b24 | max(⌈a/3⌉, c) |
| b12 | max(⌈a/2⌉, c) |
| b9 | ⌈c/2⌉, and only if a = 0 |

- b12 and b24 end the same fractions; b24 can be shorter when 2s dominate
  (1/8 = 0.γ₂₄ = 0.16₁₂).
- b9 is about twice as short on pure powers of 3 (1/81 = 0.01₉, four digits in b24).
- After n b10 digits, the leftover denominator is 2^max(a−n, 0)·3ᶜ. If n ≥ a, a b9 tail
  is the shorter choice. If n < a, a b9 tail repeats and only b24 (or more b10 digits)
  can end it.

Worked example, 5/432 (432 = 2⁴·3³):

- b24: 0.αηρ (0.06G₂₄), since 5/432 × 24³ = 160 = 6·24 + 16.
- b10 + b9: 0.0115♄♄. Four b10 digits clear 2⁴, leaving 20/27 = 0.66₉.
- b10 + b24: 0.0115στρ. 20/27 × 24³ = 10240 = 17·576 + 18·24 + 16.
- dec/time tom layout (10, 10, 10, 9, 10, 24): 0.011♃1ρ.
- 5/432 d = 1000 SI s.

## Fractions of a day

| fraction | b10 | b12 | b10 + b9 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1/2 | 0.5 | 0.6 | 0.5 |
| 1/3 | 0.333… | 0.4 | 0.♁ |
| 1/5 | 0.2 | 0.2497… | 0.2 |
| 1/6 | 0.1666… | 0.2 | 0.1♄ |
| 1/9 | 0.111… | 0.14 | 0.☿ |
| 1/10 | 0.1 | 0.12497… | 0.1 |
| 1/12 | 0.08333… | 0.1 | 0.08♁ |

b12 is shorter for the thirds family; b10 + b9 wins on whether a fraction ends at all and
keeps percentages and metric units clean.

## Why b9 is the right complement for b10

- It adds only the missing prime. A b6 or b12 tail would waste capacity on 2s that b10
  already handles, and each b9 digit absorbs two factors of 3.
- A b9 digit g equals the b10 digit g repeated forever from its slot, because
  g/9 = 0.ggg…: 0.♁ = 0.333…, 0.1♄ = 0.1666…, 0.08♁ = 0.08333…. Later digits add on
  top. There is no glyph for 9 because 0.999… = 1 is a carry. Only b9 turns decimal's
  repeating tails into single glyphs, since a repeating decimal digit always means g/9.
- The same fact (10 ≡ 1 mod 9) gives decimal its digit-sum tests for 3 and 9
  ("casting out nines"): 4 + 3 + 2 = 9, so 9 divides 432. Decimal is already
  "9-aware".
- In its slot's unit a b9 glyph is worth g × 10/9, at most 0.89 above g, so it reads
  almost like a decimal digit. A b24 letter is worth g × 10/24 (ω = 9.58), far from
  its index.
- A b9 slot holds log₁₀ 9 ≈ 0.95 of a decimal digit's information, so swapping a b10
  digit for a b9 digit costs almost nothing. A b24 slot holds about 1.38 decimal
  digits.
- Note: 9 < 10 does not decide whether a glyph fits a slot; Dec's convention does. The
  b24 sid digit also fills one slot.
- Separate glyphs make the radix visible. Dozenal "10" means twelve, so a dozenal
  numeral is ambiguous unless you know the base; Dec never changes what a decimal digit
  means.

## Finger tricks

![9 × 8 = ♅2: fold finger 8, then count the fingers to its left in b9 and to its right in
b10. Adapted from [Multiplication by 9
mnemonic.svg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Multiplication_by_9_mnemonic.svg) by
CMG Lee, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0).](/dec/time/b9fingers.svg){#fig-b9fingers}

To multiply n by 9, fold finger n. Since 9n = 10(n − 1) + (10 − n), the n − 1 fingers to
its left are the tens digit and the 10 − n fingers to its right are the ones digit. When the
fingers on the left are counted in b9 and those on the right in b10, the result is a b9
glyph followed by a b10 digit.

**b10 to b9.** A decimilliday (dmd) is 9 Dec seconds, and in a tod the b9 glyph that
replaces the dmd digit counts tens of Dec seconds, followed by a Dec-second digit. So
converting a dmd digit n is 9 × n: fold finger n and read the glyph on the left and the
seconds digit on the right.

- 3753 decimillidays: fold finger 3 → ♀7, so 375♀7.
- 8 dmd: fold finger 8 → ♅2 (72 Dec seconds).
- 0 dmd → ☉0.

Later decimal digits add 0.9 s each and can carry; the finger step stays the same.

**Repeating decimals.** The finger trick converts an exact decimal digit, so it does not by
itself end a repeating decimal. For that, use the fact that a b9 glyph g is the b10 digit g
repeated forever (g/9 = 0.ggg…):

- A tail that repeats one digit becomes that glyph: 1/3 = 0.♁, 2/3 = 0.♄, and
  1 h = 0.41666… dd = 0.41♄ dd.
- A tail with a longer period becomes single-digit repeats after multiplying by 9
  (9x = 10x − x): 9 × 0.740740… = 7.407407… − 0.740740… = 6.666…, so 0.740740… =
  0.♄♄ and 5/432 = 0.011574074… = 0.0115♄♄.

**b9 to b10.** Since 10g + s = 9g + (g + s), a glyph g followed by a decimal digit s is

  g + (g + s)/9

of the slot the glyph replaced: write g, then add (g + s) repeated forever, carrying when
g + s ≥ 9.

- g + s = 9 (the digit-sum test): exactly g + 1. On the hands, g fingers up on the left and
  s on the right leave one finger folded, and its number is the answer: ♀7 → finger 3 → 3
  dmd, ♅2 → 8 dmd.
- Otherwise the remainder repeats: ♀8 → 2 + 10/9 = 3.111… dmd (375♀8 = 37531.1… cmd);
  ♀3 → 2 + 5/9 = 2.555… dmd.
- A glyph on its own is its digit repeated: 0.41♄ = 0.41666….

## Why b24 is in Dec at all

- b24 adds no prime that b10 + b9 lacks; it only packs 2³·3 into one glyph.
- Its job is matching hms units: 86400 = 2⁷·3³·5². A tod with four b10 digits, one b9
  digit, and one b24 digit has 10⁴·9·24 = 2160000 = 25 × 86400 slots per day.
- Without b24, b10 + b9 needs seven b10 digits and two b9 digits (9 digits instead of 6):
  10⁷·9² ÷ 86400 = 9375.
- For whole hours, b24 needs one digit; b10 + b9 needs four (1 h = 41♄ decimillidays,
  0.041♄ d).
- If Dec never had to match hms or SI seconds, b24 would be unnecessary.

## What b12 still has

- One uniform radix for all arithmetic. b10 + b9 is mixed radix: great for representing
  quantities, awkward for computing. Adding numerals whose b9 glyphs sit in different
  slots needs conversion, and a product of numerals with k₁ and k₂ b9 digits needs
  k₁ + k₂ b9 digits in new slots, with no single multiplication table. hms has the same
  limitation.
- Shorter thirds (0.4 vs 0.♁ is a tie; 0.1 vs 0.08♁ is not).
- Last-digit divisibility tests for 2, 3, 4, and 6.
- Costs: 1/5 and 1/10 repeat, and a 144-entry table in which familiar digit strings mean
  new things.

## Other bases

- b60 (Babylonian): same set of ending fractions as b10 + b9 in one uniform radix, but
  60 symbols. Each cuneiform digit was built from tens and units, a decimal/senary mix
  inside each digit.
- b30: smallest base with 2, 3, and 5; 900-entry table.
- b6 (seximal): tiny table, halves and thirds, no fifths.
- b20 (Maya): 2²·5, no 3. The Maya long count was mixed radix (20, 18, 20, 20).
- b2, b16: for machines.

## Why nobody used b9 before (as far as I know)

1. b9 on its own can't write 1/2, so anyone judging it as a full base drops it. Its
   value appears only as a complement.
2. Mixed radix historically came from units (12 inches, 60 minutes, £sd with 12 pence
   per shilling and 20 shillings per pound), chosen one unit at a time, not from asking
   which digit set completes b10.
3. The closest precedent is Roman: decimal integers and duodecimal fractions (unciae)
   with their own symbols. That is Dec's design with 12 instead of 9.
4. Decimal fractions are fairly recent (Stevin, 1585). Metrication pushed toward pure
   decimal; reformers who wanted 3s (dozenal societies from the 1940s) tried to replace
   the base rather than add to it.
5. Calculators made repeating decimals harmless, except where exactness and readability
   matter, like clocks.

## Verdict

- General arithmetic: b12 has a real but modest edge on thirds, paid for with fifths,
  tenths, and a costly break from habit.
- Measurement and labelling: b10 + b9 beats b12. It reaches b60 divisibility, keeps
  every decimal digit's meaning, and shows the radix through distinct glyphs.
- b24 is justified only by alignment with hms or SI seconds.
- The one argument dozenalists keep: a single uniform radix makes computation simpler.
